title: stage-boundary-clockwork-probe
summary: Field notes from an exploratory tracing run instrumenting stage boundaries across the serving runtime. Goal: quantify p50/p95/p99 contributions per stage and verify whether batch wait states or KV cache misses dominate tail latency for mixed traffic.
body:
Purpose:
This notebook documents the 'clockwork probe' experiment: lightweight instrumentation added to stage boundaries (tokenize, pre-batch, batch-wait, kv-lookup, forward, post-process, emit) and a sampled TX run across production-like traffic in a staging fleet. The experiment tests two hypotheses: (1) p99 is dominated by batching wait/eviction interactions, (2) KV cache miss penalty is amplified by long-seq requests and causes multi-hop tail amplification.

Quick findings (high level):
- End-to-end quantiles (aggregate mix): p50=46ms, p95=172ms, p99=410ms.
- For short-seqlen cohort (<=64 tokens): p50=38ms, p95=120ms, p99=240ms.
- For long-seqlen cohort (>512 tokens): p50=220ms, p95=820ms, p99=1,400ms.
- Per-stage tail contributors (aggregate): batch-wait and forward account for ~72% of p99. KV-lookup (miss path) adds a multiplicative penalty on long sequences.

Experiment setup:
- Fleet: staging cluster S-45 (4x A100-80GB per node), 16 nodes, autoscaler disabled to keep steady capacity.
- Model: open-variant v2.1 (16-bit, kv-cache enabled, synchronous forward).
- Traffic: replay of 200k requests sampled from last 48h production traces (mix: 68% short, 24% mid, 8% long).
- Instrumentation: added millisecond-resolution timers at stage entry/exit for: tokenize, pre-batch (input normalization), batch-wait (time waiting for batch to form), kv-lookup (including local cache hit/miss tag), forward (model compute), post-process, emit (serialization + egress). Traces sampled at 2% overall, full-stage spans captured for that sample.
- Sampling method: deterministic sampling by route hash to preserve cohort proportions; extra 1% targeted sampling for >512 seqlen requests.

Collection notes:
- Trace recorder appended a stage tag boolean 'kv_miss' when the local key lookup returned miss and remote sharded fetch occurred.
- Batch composition logs included batch size distribution and waiting time per batch.
- We correlated trace IDs with batch IDs to reconstruct which requests shared a batch.

Aggregate quantiles (end-to-end):
- p50: 46ms
- p95: 172ms
- p99: 410ms
- mean: 85ms
- stdev: 120ms (skewed by long sequence tail)

Per-stage contributions (aggregate p50/p95/p99 in ms):
- Tokenize: 3 / 6 / 12
- Pre-batch (normalization): 2 / 5 / 10
- Batch-wait: 6 / 48 / 210
- KV-lookup (overall): 9 / 28 / 110
  - KV-hit path: 4 / 10 / 22
  - KV-miss path (remote fetch): 48 / 160 / 420 (observed only in ~6% of sampled requests; disproportionately in long cohort)
- Forward (model compute): 20 / 70 / 150
- Post-process: 4 / 8 / 18
- Emit (serialization + egress): 2 / 7 / 18

Observations and interpretation:
1) Batch-wait tail is bimodal. Most batches form in <15ms, but a small fraction of batches wait >150ms. These long waits correlate with head-of-line requests that contain long seqlens or are pinned to a single node due to routing affinity.
2) KV-miss remote fetches create large outliers (see KV-miss path). Though rare, they compound with batch-wait and large forward times to create the heaviest tails. The multiplicative stacking is: KV-miss (remote fetch) -> larger forward (more tokens) -> longer emit.
3) Long sequences dominate p99 despite being only ~8% of traffic. For long cohort, the forward stage is the largest absolute contributor, but batch-wait and KV-miss determine whether these long-forward requests end up in the p99 bucket.
4) There is evidence of cross-request interference inside the batcher: when a long request enters a batch, per-token forward gets stretched due to NVLink contention and CUDA scheduler preemption on a small subset of hosts.

Microcase examples (selected traces):
- Trace A (short request, kv-hit): 34ms total — batch-wait 4ms, forward 18ms, rest small.
- Trace B (long request, kv-miss, late-batch): 1,380ms total — batch-wait 180ms, kv-remote 420ms, forward 600ms, emit 90ms.
- Trace C (mid request, kv-hit, host contention): 560ms total — batch-wait 220ms (batch formed late), forward 200ms (cuda contention spike), post-process 20ms.

Immediate mitigations and quick experiments tried during probe:
- Reduced max-batch-wait threshold from 250ms -> 120ms (trial on 10% of nodes): p95 improved ~12% for mixed traffic, p99 improved ~6% for short cohort but had minimal effect on long-cohort p99.
- Enabled a lightweight KV-prefetch heuristic for requests with expected long seqlen (heuristic based on route + historical seqlen): KV-miss rate for targeted cohort decreased from 6.3% -> 2.0% on trial nodes; end-to-end p99 for targeted cohort improved ~18%.
- Pin long-seq traffic to dedicated forward lanes (separate CUDA streams / reserved GPUs): reduced contention events in measured hosts but needs capacity planning.

Recommendations (next steps):
1) Expand targeted KV-prefetch: build a server-side profile that predicts seqlen at admission and triggers async prefetch for likely long requests. Create ticket JIRA-ENG-9942.
2) Add per-batch early-release heuristic: if a batch contains a single long request and the current batch wait exceeds X ms, release smaller sub-batches to avoid head-of-line tail amplification. Prototype flag: batch_early_release=true.
3) Hard limit on batch-wait for low-latency routes: lower default max_wait for routes flagged as low-latency SLAs; keep conservative wait on throughput-optimized routes.
4) Investigate NVLink/CUDA scheduling instrumentation: correlate kernel timelines with trace IDs on hosts exhibiting contention to confirm interference hypothesis.
5) Long-cohort capacity plan: simulate reserving 8–12% capacity as dedicated long-forward lanes and run cost/latency tradeoff analysis.

Open questions and risks:
- Prefetch correctness: ensure async KV-prefetch doesn't violate freshness requirements for certain customers. Need security review if prefetch touches customer-scoped cache.
- Cost of dedicated lanes: reserved GPUs increase unit cost; quantify latency benefit vs cost.
- Edge cases in early-release batching may reduce throughput; need A/B test to measure downstream per-token cost effect.

Action items and owners:
- JIRA-ENG-9942 (Ava): profiling and rollout plan for KV-prefetch heuristic.
- JIRA-ENG-9951 (Rajesh): batch early-release prototype + safety limits.
- JIRA-ENG-9959 (Sofia): host-level kernel timeline collector and correlation script.
- Follow-up checkpoint: 2 weeks after prototyping to re-run clockwork probe with same sampling to compare quantiles.

Appendix (notes for reviewers):
- Raw trace dump (2% sample) uploaded to S3: s3://redwood-staging/clockwork-probe/2025-01-18/sample-traces.ndjson (link in Confluence).
- Bench harness used: scripts/harness/clockwork_replay_v2.py (PR 2213).
- Visualization: Per-stage stacked violin plots and cohort CDFs created in the staging notebook (link in linked_artifacts).

Notes-to-self: keep this experiment configuration reproducible — commit the fleet snapshot and sampling seed to the ticket before re-run.

-- Ava M.
